item.title: Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' after initially expressing surprise
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
[Getty Images] Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment. The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post. Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it. The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel. That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation. Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia". "Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said. The BBC has asked the White House for further details. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. "All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure. Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides. Earlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it , while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday. The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties. Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports. "Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course". Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk. On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal. The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president". Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire. The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation. Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power. Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war. Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said. One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said. item.title: 6 takeaways from often contentious South Carolina Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US Senate candidates Democrat Annie Andrews and Republican Sen. Darline Graham take notes before a debate in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters South Carolina has emerged as perhaps the most surprising Senate race to be competitive late in the 2026 midterm elections. And on Sunday night, appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian nominee Kasie Whitener took part in the only debate currently scheduled in the race. The debate was often contentious, with both Graham and Andrews taking aim at each other. Andrews focused on the idea that Graham — the late former Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom President Donald Trump plucked from obscurity to succeed him — is the choice of political insiders and not running a serious campaign. She at one point alluded to an embarrassing moment at a primary runoff debate in which Graham said, “National security is not my thing.” “If your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.” Graham also hit Andrews early and often, seeking to tie her to the political left. And she repeatedly took offense to the attacks that Andrews lodged, accusing Andrews of going after her family. Below are some takeaways from the debate. unknown content item - Graham avoided another major flub Job No. 1 for Graham was avoiding a moment like the one on national security. And she cleared that bar. At that GOP debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, she was asked a relatively basic — at least for a senator — question about US foreign policy interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. Seemingly not knowing where to go with it, she just admitted that she didn’t know much about the issue. At the same debate, she also mistakenly cited 50 million people living in South Carolina, when the actual number is less than 6 million. That doesn’t mean Sunday was smooth sailing. Graham paused awkwardly at times. She struggled to make some of her attack lines, such as on transgender rights, land. Some of her claims — like that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon before the US and Israel launched the war earlier this year — don’t actually appear true. But for a Republican running in a pretty red state, she came across as more capable than before. Republican Sen. Darline Graham reacts before a debate with Senate candidates Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian Kasie Whitener in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters Graham came out swinging That being said, Graham seemed to confirm that her campaign is quite concerned about Andrews, judging by how much time she spent attacking the Democrat. It started almost instantly, with Graham calling Andrews “most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina” in her first answer. She accused Andrews of supporting government-run healthcare, which Andrews denied. She pointed to Andrews’ past work on gun control issues. She attacked Andrews for opposing President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and for having the support of Jane Fonda’s political action committee. And after Andrews mentioned her primary runoff debate moment, Graham accused her of lying about her liberal positions. “Let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing, apparently, is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” she said. “But you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove different. Shame on you.” The attacks confirmed the competitiveness of the race. The national GOP recently turned heads by spending $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign. US Senate candidate Democrat Annie Andrews arrives for a debate with candidates Republican Darline Graham and Libertarian Kasie Whitener in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters Andrews distanced herself from the Democratic Party and the left But Andrews had a pretty memorable answer for much of it. “She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie Ocasio Mamdani; that’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said, referring to a trio of democratic socialist lawmakers. “But the truth is: My name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.” Graham opted not to use her married name — Darline Graham Nordone — when she was appointed as a senator. “My legal name is Graham and has always been Graham,” she said. “And you know why it’s Graham? Because I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them.” At another point in the debate, Andrews said that “both parties have failed on immigration” and that “Democrats have failed on the border.” Andrews added: “And the truth is, I support the Second Amendment. I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law, and yes, I want to lower taxes on the middle class.” Graham tries to make transgender attacks land Few attacks have been as central to the race as the GOP’s efforts to focus on transgender issues. Just in the last week, Trump posted on social media using an anti-transgender slur for Andrews, and Andrews launched a direct-to-camera ad defending herself on the issue. But if you blinked, you might have missed it Sunday night. Graham brought it up twice, but only briefly. And she did so both times at the end of an answer, right before the debate quickly moved on. That included at the very end of the debate. “But let’s talk about a couple of other concerns I have — that she’s deceiving the people of South Carolina with these transgender issues,” Graham said in the final words of the night. The debate moderator quickly signaled the debate had to end there, and it was over. That was a win for Andrews, in that she didn’t really have to answer for the issue — or explain her 2022 comments on social media calling a state law banning transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams at public schools “shameful.” Graham defended the Iran war Andrews repeatedly pointed to Graham declining to vote with Democrats and a few Republicans to bringing the Iran war to an end, noting Graham has had three chances to do so. Graham responded by claiming that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon — which is not backed up by known US intelligence. But unlike some GOP Senate candidates who have said the war needs to end, she went a little further in defending the need to give Trump more time. She argued Iran is being strangled financially. “Why in the world would we stop now when they are still dangerous and we are close to ending the war?” Graham said. “Again, I think the president wants to end the war. I know he does. We all want the war to end. But I support a strong military. I believe in peace through strength.” US Senate candidate Democrat Annie Andrews takes notes before a debate with Republican US Sen. Darline Graham and US Senate Libertarian candidate Kasie Whitener in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters Few mentions of Trump Few things loomed as large over the debate as Trump; his unpopularity is a major reason South Carolina and other deep-red states are as competitive this fall. But he wasn’t a major focus. There was the occasional mention of something Trump has done, but he wasn’t really a focal point for anybody. In fact, the word “Trump” was only uttered a handful of times. Graham mentioned the president just a few times, praising him for creating an AI task force and waiving restrictions on red-dye diesel . Even when Andrews was arguing Graham was the pick of insiders, she didn’t actually cite the one insider above all who elevated Graham: Trump. And when talking about the war, she generally didn’t attach it to the president. That perhaps shouldn’t be too surprising from the Democrat. While Trump is broadly unpopular nationwide, this is still a state he won by 18 points in 2024. item.title: Democrats are making corruption messaging a pocketbook issue
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats may be discovering the political power of calling something rigged. They’re leaning hard into anti-corruption messaging in the final weeks of the campaign as new research suggests that linking corruption to Americans’ economic struggles can boost Democrats into the home stretch. Messaging from Democrats that tied corruption to housing, health care and the cost of living increased voter support for Democratic congressional candidates by about 3 percentage points, according to a national survey last month conducted by Blue Rose Research and Democratic-aligned Winning Jobs Narrative Action, which was obtained by POLITICO . The findings align with a shift in how Democrats are talking about corruption — and help explain why that message has exploded on the campaign trail. From Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia to James Talarico in Texas and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Democrats have zeroed in on a common argument: Washington is rigged to benefit the wealthy at the expense of everyday Americans. “We have a corruption crisis in this country, and it is leading to an affordability crisis,” Iowa Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek said during his Senate debate against Rep. Ashley Hinson last week. It’s a message that is reverberating across campaigns. In a recent presentation delivered to Democratic groups on Capitol Hill, longtime Democratic strategist Jesse Ferguson offered a succinct playbook: “Corruption is why your costs are high,” according to the presentation viewed by POLITICO. His presentation also encouraged Democrats to lead with the acknowledgement that costs are high and then go into corruption, acknowledge that it happens across parties and avoid making President Donald Trump the sole focus of their attacks. “Trump works as an example of corruption that raises costs, not as the whole case,” the presentation said. Since April, Democratic candidates and outside groups in House and Senate races have spent roughly $104 million on advertising mentioning corruption, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. Republicans, meanwhile, have spent $36 million across House and Senate campaigns over the same period. “It’s not just like, ‘oh, look at what’s happening with the ballroom,’ or ‘boy, Donald Trump’s made a lot of money on crypto,’” Democratic strategist Chris Meagher said. "You have to be able to tie it to the impact on people’s lives." “The narrative works best when it’s an outsider candidate who is linking a rigged economy to a rigged political system,” longtime Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said of the anti-corruption messaging. Running against corruption is not new. But as Democrats looked for a way out of the political wilderness after 2024, they began turning a familiar attack — anti-corruption — into a broader message tied to voters’ economic pain. What once was an attack largely focused on Trump has become a more expansive argument for candidates trying to connect it to why Americans are struggling financially, potentially providing a blueprint for the party beyond November. “Democrats used to talk about corruption as a crime. Now corruption is the explanation for costs,” Ferguson, the Democratic strategist, said. The issue — and messaging around it — is also coming to the fore in a cycle when anger over the suppression of Epstein files hit a fever pitch and public pressure to ban Congress from trading stocks continues to mount. And it’s not just the research by Blue Rose that shows the potential potency of that message. In another recent survey from the Democratic group Navigator Research , obtained by POLITICO, the vast majority of Americans — both Democrats and Republicans — say corruption is driving up their costs. That same survey of registered voters, conducted in August, found majorities, including roughly a quarter of Republicans, say Trump is bringing more corruption to Washington than fixing it. And new results from the nonpartisan Center Square’s Voter Voice Poll, conducted this month by Noble Predictive Insights and shared first with POLITICO, show 10% of voters ranking government corruption as the second most important issue facing Americans, tied with the economy and jobs, and only behind inflation and price increases. In some instances, Democrats have wrested the word “rigged” away from Trump who has used it in the context of unproven election fraud and turned it into a mobilizing political talking point. That’s a departure from March 2024 when Democrats criticized then Rep. Katie Porter for accusing special interests of spending money to “rig” the California Senate race after she lost in the state’s primary. But now some Democrats are embracing that language as a way to rail against what they see as a corrupt system. “They’re rigging the rules to benefit their wealthy donors and corporate special interests,” former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown said in a message to supporters announcing the launch of his campaign to return to office. But the corruption resonates across parties. Republicans who spoke with POLITICO said Democrats do not own the issue — voters everywhere are animated by it. While polling shows that voters in both major parties believe the government is corrupt , Republicans accuse Democrats of lacking credibility on the issue. “Americans have been disgusted by the level of self-serving corruption that spread like herpes through the slimy politicians who run the Democrat Party, and now they’re suddenly changing their tune because it’s an election year,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Mike Marinella said in a statement. “Voters see through the facade, and they know Republicans are cleaning up the rot left behind by Democrat leaders.” On the Senate side, National Republican Senatorial Committee spokesperson Bernadette Breslin pointed POLITICO to a poll in Minnesota — a rare offensive opportunity for Senate Republicans this cycle — that shows there are just about as many voters who blame Democratic Gov. Tim Walz for widespread fraud of federally-funded government programs in the state as there are who blame the criminals. Walz’s lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, is running for Senate against Republican Michele Tafoya, and corruption under Democratic rule is a key theme for Republicans in the race. “The overwhelming majority of Minnesotans blame the Walz-Flanagan administration — and the criminals it aided and abetted — for plundering their hard-earned taxpayer dollars,” Breslin said. “They’ll vote for Michele Tafoya to right the ship this November.” Steve Pierce, executive director at Winning Jobs Narrative Action, said one of the biggest shifts for Democrats this cycle on corruption has been a move away from a message largely rooted in concerns over democratic norms, which have struggled to break through in a way that moves voters in past cycles. “You’ve seen Democrats, rather than connecting corruption to democracy, connecting it to affordability, connecting it to the top concern that voters have,” said Pierce. “It’s connecting it in a way that’s meaningful to voters around the things that they are thinking about every day.” The anti-corruption message has played out across the country, and as an explanation for frustration against different economic pain points, including rising electric bills and local data center projects. A recent memo on data centers from House Majority PAC, the main super PAC working to elect House Democrats, noted the “message environment in the 2026 election cycle has been dominated by costs, with an important secondary theme around corruption that began to emerge last year.” The group’s spokesperson, CJ Warnke, told POLITICO that “every single poll and every single focus group shows affordability to be voters’ number one issue, and they specifically point to corrupt politicians as being responsible for driving up prices.” Next month’s midterms will offer the clearest test yet of whether Democrats can turn this message into votes. But Democratic operatives increasingly see anti-corruption messaging as more than just a short-term political weapon — as long as they try to do something about it if they win control next year. “I think the thing for Democrats, if they do want to keep it on the radar heading into 2028, and I think they should because I think it is a really potent issue for them, they are going to have to also deliver on it,” said Pierce. “They have to be able to show up to get caught trying,” he said. item.title: Trump's deal to buy Russian diesel draws rare bipartisan rebuke
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Donald Trump to “immediately reverse course” on his decision to allow Russian diesel imports, accusing the administration of violating federal law and handing Moscow a financial lifeline as it wages war against Ukraine. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” the senators said in a statement released Sunday , citing Congress’ 2022 ban on Russian energy imports. “The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.” The rebuke includes four Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Thom Tillis (N.C.) and John Curtis (Utah) — along with Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Ron Wyden (Ore.). Shaheen is the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel “to the American and Global Marketplace” following a discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Treasury Department subsequently issued a general license allowing Russian diesel imports into the U.S. through April 2027. The move comes as Trump scrambles to try to bring down fuel prices ahead of the midterms, with the Iran war — now in its seventh month — contributing to the surge in costs. In September, the average price of diesel hit a record $6.53 per gallon, according to AAA . “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” the senators wrote. “The Administration must immediately reverse course.” Tillis, a Republican who frequently splits with the Trump administration, had already questioned the deal’s legality Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” pointing to the 2022 law’s conditions for lifting the import ban, including a full Russian withdrawal from Ukraine. “I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis said. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory they occupied.” The White House, responding to Tillis’ earlier criticism, pointed POLITICO to a Trump Truth Social post declaring “an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine.” The president provided no details or evidence that Moscow had agreed. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the senators’ joint statement. The diesel agreement also overshadowed talks between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiators in Miami on Friday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that easing sanctions without a lasting de-escalation agreement would signal weakness. Cheyanne Daniels contributed to this reporting. item.title: Fed officials are warning of more economic pain. Many Americans already feel it.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building is seen under construction in Washington, D.C., on September 15, 2026. - Mehmet Eser/Anadolu/Getty Images Four years ago, with inflation at multi-decade highs, then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a blunt message to Americans: Getting inflation under control would come at a cost. The Fed needed to act “forcefully,” Powell told attendees at a key central banker conference that August. Doing so, he cautioned, would bring “some pain” for consumers. Now, with the Fed back to raising interest rates for the first time in three years, a familiar warning about the economic fallout is resurfacing. Inflation across the country is being driven primarily by fuel prices, which have skyrocketed since the war with Iran broke out in February. The Fed has little control over oil production, but by raising interest rates, it is seeking to prevent higher energy costs from spilling over into other parts of the economy and fueling broader inflation. A sign displays the prices of unleaded gasoline and diesel fuel as a driver refuels a vehicle at a gas station in Torrance, California, on September 28, 2026. - Caroline Brehman/Bloomberg/Getty Images While this type of supply-driven inflation may be easier to bring under control than the post-pandemic demand-driven inflation, “it won’t be painless either,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said last month. For central bankers, the challenge is balancing two competing priorities: keeping inflation in check and preserving a healthy labor market. When price increases become too rapid, the Fed typically raises interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses. That, in turn, can curb spending and cool demand, easing pressure on prices. But that slowdown can come at a cost to workers, often leading to weaker hiring, fewer job openings, and, in some cases, job losses, as businesses struggle with higher borrowing costs. “Inflation is the disease. And now the Fed comes with a cure: higher interest rates,” Beth Ann Bovino, chief economist at US Bank, said. “I don’t know which is more painful because they both hurt.” A customer shops in a supermarket in New York on September 28, 2026. - Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity, making it a key driver of growth. If Americans pull back — either because prices are eating up more of their budgets or because higher borrowing costs force them to set aside more money for expenses such as a home purchase — the economy could slow. In a worst-case scenario, that pullback could help tip the economy into a recession, Bovino told CNN. For now, though, economic pain isn’t being felt equally . Americans with substantial investments in the stock market, which is hovering near record highs , may be doing just fine. Those who rely more heavily on their paychecks to cover everyday expenses have less of a cushion against rising prices. “Those are the people being hurt,” she said. Patience is a virtue — until it isn’t With the risks of higher interest rates in mind, a growing chorus of Fed officials have recently been advocating for a more patient approach as they tackle the issue of inflation. Rather than trying to get a head start at fighting the potential for more or broader-based inflation, several central bankers have said they’d like more time to observe how economic conditions evolve to get a better idea of how many more rate hikes, if any, are needed. “There is no need for urgency,” New York Fed President John Williams said last month. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson echoed that sentiment. “Any future adjustments in policy should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks,” he said earlier this month. But waiting to act carries risks of its own. With the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge more than a percentage point above its 2% annual target, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that delaying action could make the fight against inflation even more painful. “The longer inflation stays above our objective, the harder it will be for us to bring it back down, and the more pain that individuals and businesses are going to be experiencing,” Hammack said in an August CNBC interview. For the Fed, the challenge is figuring out how much pain the economy can withstand — and which risk is worse: acting too soon or waiting too long. Either way, consumers are likely to pay the price. The September Consumer Price Index report due Wednesday may give officials some valuable clues. item.title: Rep. Omar says she will 'not be silenced,' calls Fed search of her home an 'intimidation' campaign
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed scrutiny to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid . The search of the Minnesota congresswoman's home so close to next month's midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. The Justice Department confirmed in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area in connection with an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details. The nature and scope of the investigation were unclear, though officials in President Donald Trump's administration have repeatedly hinted at the existence of an inquiry targeting Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have repeatedly drawn criticism from Republicans and senior Trump officials. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that there was an "ongoing investigation" related in part to whether Omar lied on her immigration forms and that "something's going to happen." Omar responded to the search with a statement on X that called it an "attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she said. "I will not be silenced." Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search of her home took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot for reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. "For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," top House Democratic leaders said in a statement. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family." Trump has frequently targeted Omar Trump as recently as this past weekend brought up Omar at a rally in Tennessee, where he attacked her upbringing and suggested that Vice President JD Vance "and our people" were investigating her. Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud — an allegation she has denied — and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate her. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department. The Justice Department said in a statement that Monday's enforcement action "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation." The street was blocked off Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home. Omar has long been a target for Republicans Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota's 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress. When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks. In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced recently to 14 months in prison. Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies." "It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance told reporters in May. "So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime." In a separate interview with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that "we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America." He said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had been discussing it and "trying to look at what the remedies are." "That's the thing that we're trying to figure out," he said. "What are the legal remedies now that we know that she's committed immigration fraud. How do you go after her? How do you investigate her? How do you actually do the thing? How do you build the case necessary to get some, some, some justice for the American people?" Omar's office has defended her against past allegations Omar's office in March dismissed Vance's claims as fabricated and defamatory. "This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to 'create stories' to redirect the media," Omar's chief of staff, Connor McNutt, said in a statement. "This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party's unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers," McNutt said at the time of the vice president's allegations and comments. ___ Associated Press writers Lisa Mascaro, Michelle L. Price and River Zhang in Washington, Kathy McCormack in Concord, N.H., Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pa., and Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., contributed. item.title: Drone swarms are a problem Secret Service says they have not solved yet
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Secret Service is working out how to handle threats that have evolved beyond a lone gunman to attack drones. Deputy Director Matthew Quinn is leading the agency's new multimillion-dollar program to develop offensive and defensive drone capabilities. Among the new tools in the agency's arsenal is an artificial intelligence and radar-guided drone hunter, which disables enemy drones and captures them with a net. "Swarms are a huge problem and a big threat," Quinn said. "I'd love to tell you the swarm problem is solved. It's not. I will tell you that at the White House, White House is the safest place on Earth." Drones and the Secret Service The war in Ukraine has become a testing ground for the weaponization of drones . And that hasn't gone unnoticed by the Secret Service. "We know that technology is going to hit the homeland at some point," Quinn said. "So we're using lessons learned there to build our program and make sure we're ahead of it before it gets here." It's about planning ahead, Secret Service Director Sean Curran said. "We have to assume that it's possible," Curran said. "The second we're not, we're going to get caught flat-footed." The concern is that a small, rudimentary drone could be weaponized with explosives and do serious damage to a large concert, sporting event or campaign rally. 60 Minutes has learned the Secret Service used electronic jamming equipment to take down a drone at the December Army-Navy game, where the president and members of Congress were in attendance. Confronting a rise in threats to protectees The Secret Service is confronting both new types and a rising number of threats. There have been 10,000 threats made against Secret Service protectees so far this year; it's a 40% year over year increase in cases involving full-time protectees, according to Curran. "I think a lot of it has to do with the internet," he said. "You know, people are more accessible. Information is more accessible." Mr. Trump, one of the most polarizing political figures in American history, has survived several attempts on his life, including at a Butler, Pennsylvania, campaign rally , at his Florida golf course , and at the White House Correspondents' Dinner . "I would say there's people on both sides of the aisle that either love or hate any president. I think the biggest factor we're dealing with today is mental health issues for sure," Quinn said. "More people are being pushed over the edge in either direction." The agency doesn't look at which side of the political aisle threats come from, Curran said. Research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan, nonprofit policy research organization, showed a spike in incidents from the left in 2025. It was the first time the number of attacks from the left have been higher than right-wing attacks in 30 years. This year, that trend has reversed, with more attacks coming from the right so far. The Secret Service is also dealing with threats coming from outside the country, including threats from Iran . Top leaders there have vowed revenge against the U.S. for the killing of their supreme leader. "Turn on the TV and you can see the funeral where there are massive banners saying 'Kill President Trump.' So do we recognize the threat environment has increased? Absolutely," Quinn said. "How we do it and how we change, that's where we prefer to stay in the background." Changes at Secret Service The Secret Service has undergone internal changes in recent years after facing backlash for its failure to prevent Thomas Crooks' attempt on Mr. Trump's life in Butler in 2024. Curran was the lead agent in charge of protecting Mr. Trump that day. He said he had requested additional resources for the event, but that he'd "rather not get into the past." Kimberly Cheatle , who was head of the Secret Service during the Butler incident, stepped down. When Mr. Trump's second term began, he appointed Curran as head of the agency. This past June, the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General released a report on Butler . It found the Secret Service "missed multiple opportunities to detect, prevent, and disrupt the assassination attempt." Curran, guiding several changes at the agency, said he's convinced nothing like the day's events will happen again. Many candidates are now in training for the Secret Service, which has been dangerously understaffed for years. A Homeland Security Inspector General's report found the counter-sniper team is staffed 73% below the level needed to protect the nation's most senior leaders. There are 942 people in training today compared to "maybe 200" last year, Quinn said. And with the president back on the campaign trail ahead of the midterm elections , Curran has added new training for agents to avoid the mistakes of Butler. Even the president's limousine is getting regular updates, most of them classified. It weighs up to 10 tons, with bulletproof glass and defensive countermeasures. "I don't want to get into its capabilities. But it can do a lot," Curran said. He's added a medical response truck, housing a trauma unit and a field surgeon ready to treat gunshot wounds. There's also a new armored personnel carrier in the president's motorcade. "When you look at some of the significant civil disturbance events we've had, how do you move people? You look at getting teams to the Capitol during the January 6th event. This provides us the ability to get people where they need to be and take care of them. Keep them safe," Quinn said. "The mission is to protect the president of the United States" That protection extends to the new Air Force One , a 747 donated by the Middle Eastern country of Qatar. It cost the U.S. nearly $400 million to add security enhancements to that plane, according to the U.S. Air Force. Curran said the plane is trusted, but declined to explain what was behind that trust. Despite his confidence, the Secret Service would not let the president fly home on that plane from Turkey in July after intelligence reports of an Iranian plot to fire a missile at the presidential jet. Mr. Trump was secretly slipped away to another plane, while Cabinet members, White House staff, the press and Secret Service agents were left on the decoy plane — the old Air Force One. "That's not the first time we've done that," Curran said. "We wish that wasn't reported, because that takes some of our tactics away from being able to do something similar again. It certainly wasn't the first time where we did something like that." Curran wouldn't specifically say whether Mr. Trump had been on a decoy plane on other occasions. Quinn stressed that the focus is on keeping the president safe. "When you're operating in any protective detail with the president of the United States, for any president, the priority is the president," Quinn said. "Everyone else — staff, agents, media, personnel involved — are not the priority, including our own personnel. As hard as that may be for some to understand, the mission is to protect the president of the United States." item.title: Mike Johnson says he has no plans to step aside if Republicans lose the House
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Speaker Mike Johnson said he intends to serve as GOP leader if Republicans lose their House majority in November — but he remains bullish about the party's chances despite significant headwinds. "In the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government," Johnson told CBS News' Robert Costa in an interview near Johnson's hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana. Johnson, who has led House Republicans as speaker since 2023, has repeatedly pushed back on questions about his plans if the GOP loses the majority in the lower chamber in November. Known for his optimistic outlook, the speaker has expressed confidence that Republicans will hold on to the chamber, or even grow their narrow majority. But midterm dynamics traditionally boost the party opposing the party in control of the White House, and the unpopular war in Iran, high gas and diesel prices and other controversial Trump administration policies have added to those challenges for the GOP. Last week, a comment Johnson made to Fox News on his plans for his future fueled speculation that he could retire from politics, as he suggested that he could go back to his hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business if the GOP loses the House majority. "It's just hilarious," Johnson said of the interest the comment spurred, telling Costa that the remark was "tongue in cheek." "What I was trying to say to them is that throughout my whole life, my number one objective is to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country, and that's always what I've thought," Johnson said. "And I was trying to make the point that if God has a different design, then we'll follow that. But what I believe is, I'm going to be the speaker of the House for at least two more years." But Johnson added, "If, heaven forbid, we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in divided government." "My intention is to stay and serve, and that's what I've been doing, as best I can," he said. Johnson has been campaigning heavily in recent weeks, with plans to hit 40 districts in 22 states before polls close on Election Day. He made a case for his continued leadership — whether in the majority or the minority — pointing to the millions of dollars he's brought in for Republicans this cycle, his busy travel schedule, and his work to corral a sometimes volatile GOP majority in this Congress. "I'm not sure what the case would be for any alternative," he said. "I intend to stay and lead." When pressed by Costa on whether he has it in him to be a tough, combative minority leader in the current political environment, Johnson pointed to his time on the House Judiciary Committee and his defense of President Trump during his two impeachment trials. "I was a litigator in my past life — constitutional law attorney. We can be tough, but we can be happy warriors," he said. "That's what Ronald Reagan was. That's what I fashioned myself as." But Johnson was clear: he has "no intention other than winning this majority and serving as speaker." "That is what's going to happen," Johnson said. "And I'm telling you, I'm leaving it all in the field to do it." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/mike-johnson-republican-leader-midterms-2026/

item.title: Some ranchers question Trump’s policies as industry faces rising costs
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports [Yvette Mannon] Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year. In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines. Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed. With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000. On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year. Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold. The cattle market tanked immediately. 'It felt like a betrayal' "So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry." "It just felt like a betrayal," she said. Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain. That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances. Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race. Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months. Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs [Getty Images] The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices. And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive. Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle. "All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas. Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing. Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own. Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market [BBC/Lori Potter] The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry. But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning. "Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head. Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day. "It really makes a guy think," he said. A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left. But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market. "People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said. 'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business' Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall. "The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit." Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago. But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said. He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball [BBC/Lori Potter] Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms. But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate. That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago. Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper. He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts. That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry. "Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News. An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy". Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical". Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry [BBC] But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt. "We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it." But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction". [BBC] What are the US midterms? A simple guide The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things". But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed. "Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste." Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste" [BBC] Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions. "I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said. Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture." Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said. Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later. But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter. Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter [BBC] "It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in. He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers. "I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'" Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state. "They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore." Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state [Lori Potter] All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on. On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction. Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - do not pause for politics. Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude. "People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it." item.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win 2026 Nobel prize in economics
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
STOCKHOLM (AP) — American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. "The laureates' research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before," the Nobel committee wrote in a paper explaining the economists' work. "It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall, 83, is affiliated with Stanford University in California. Woodford, who was born in 1955, is affiliated with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: "It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise." Duo overturned earlier economic assumptions For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering interest rates and taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. "This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn't," said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the " stagflation '' of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. "Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,'' the Nobel committee wrote. "Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird's eye view," Hall and Woodford's research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy." Hall studied consumer choices Hall studied the way that consumers' decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. "If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,'' the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. Hall found that forecasting future consumer spending is virtually impossible. The idea that consumption is mostly unpredictable "is not good news for forecasters, or policymakers," Olivier Blanchard, who was chief economist at the International Monetary Fund during the 2008 financial crisis, said by email. "But it is news they must take into account in thinking about the effects of policy." Hall also explored the idea that some households are so strapped financially that they can't borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future "while the rest lived hand to mouth," the committee wrote. "The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead," Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. Woodford analyzed how businesses make decisions Woodford's research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. "If the business believes that its competitors' prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation," the Nobel committee wrote. "Businesses' decisions are thus also governed by their expectations." Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide "clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do." Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing. The new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has said the trend toward such "forward guidance" went too far. He's trying to scale back how much the U.S. central bank talks about its thinking and its intentions. Woodford's research also offered guidance on how central banks should respond to energy price shocks — like the one that followed the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran in February — that can both feed inflation and send unemployment higher. "Unlike the traditional Keynesian models, Woodford's model recommends a cooling measure, such as increased interest rates, to avoid uncontrolled inflation," the Nobel committee wrote. "His insight has made it possible to respond to recent supply shocks more effectively than during the oil crises of the 1970s." During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed "the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending." The winners did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press. Economics prize is last Nobel announcement this year The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896. Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine , physics , chemistry , literature and peace. Monday's award was the second Nobel win for a Stanford University professor this year. Dr. Karl Deisseroth shared the medicine prize with Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work that led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization. ___ Wiseman reported from Washington. Dazio reported from Berlin. Associated Press Writer Wyatte Grantham-Philips in Chicago contributed to this report. ___ AP Nobel Prizes: https://apnews.com/hub/nobel-prizes This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/nobel-memorial-prize-economics-awarded-054014824.html

item.title: Trump's midterm road show reveals GOP troubles — and his own priorities
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump’s whirlwind travel itinerary this month reflects a careful calculation as Republicans brace for midterm losses: where he can mobilize his most devoted supporters, where his low approval ratings make him a liability and where he can simply have a good time. His packed agenda reflects political strategy, travel logistics and the reality that the president - despite being far more active on the campaign trail than his predecessor - is an 80-year-old man with a country to run, people around him say. Trump insists on signing off on the list of places he is visiting each week, according to two people with knowledge of the process. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Trump has publicly floated a visit to Maine, where GOP Sen. Susan Collins is in a tight reelection fight, but White House and outside advisers to the president say such a trip is highly unlikely. Two people involved in planning his schedule said there are no trips scheduled to Maine or New Hampshire. Last week’s stops included deep-red Nebraska, where the Senate race is closer than once expected; Texas, for the second time in seven days; Upstate New York, to stump for his friend, gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who trails by double digits in many polls; and Tennessee, for a rally near a military base. While in Syracuse, New York, Trump brought former professional boxer Mike Tyson onto the stage to speak. Bad weather forced him to cancel a trip to Alabama for a college football game, which would have been his second visit to the state in just over a week. Football games are more fun for him than rallies, said one Trump adviser, who like others working on the president’s midterm strategy, was not authorized to discuss the matter publicly. But the rallies - now often held in smaller venues than in years past - still serve as an escape for Trump as he presides over an unpopular war and faces his lowest approval ratings in office. When he traveled to Oklahoma earlier this month, he said he was doing so “to thank them” for supporting him. In Clarksville, Tennessee, Trump said giving frequent speeches is “easy” because “there’s such love in these rooms.” “It’s amazing when you stand up here. It’s just, like, the love,” he told the crowd. “I could say the stupidest things and you clap. ” “It’s the last time he’s really going to be able to do this in full force,” said Mark Mitchell, a politically independent pollster who previously supported Trump but is now critical of many of his policies. “A 30-day blitz of the country to do these rallies again when he’s the most unpopular president - it just doesn’t really make sense.” Trump has at times been in high spirits while traveling and said he thinks campaigning is going well, one adviser said. But another person with knowledge of his behavior observed that Trump has been in a “foul mood.” Trump’s advisers maintain that the rallies are the most effective thing Trump can do - short of lowering gas prices driven up by the war he started with Iran - to try to minimize Republican losses this fall. GOP officials say Trump showing up in the backyard of supporters who voted for him three times is the party’s best chance to turn out those voters this fall when he isn’t on the ballot. Republican enthusiasm is trailing that of Democrats. A recent survey by the nonpartisan Pew Research Center found that among those who say they are extremely motivated to vote, Democrats lead 59 percent to 35 percent. That’s a contrast with the 2022 midterms, when such extremely motivated voters were evenly divided between the two parties. Supporters who sign up to attend the rallies submit their contact information to Trump’s political operation, which follows up with communications urging them to vote. Many of Trump’s supporters aren’t accustomed to voting in midterms or need to be reminded there’s an election this year, another adviser said, and all attention helps - especially in an election cycle where Democrats are highly mobilized. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, political director Matt Brasseaux and former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair - now working as an outside adviser with Trump’s political operation - have worked together to decide where Trump can be most useful, according to a person with knowledge of the process. Determining where Trump can help has been trickier in House races than in Senate contests, several of which are competitive in states Trump easily won, the person said. Some House races are so tight that Republicans worry an unpopular Trump could hurt their efforts, while statewide races can more easily benefit from the president helping boost turnout in conservative enclaves. This week, Trump is scheduled to visit Youngstown, Ohio, where the GOP under Trump has made significant gains; Wasilla, Alaska, a Republican stronghold north of Anchorage; and the heavily conservative areas of Bullhead City, Arizona, and Kalispell, Montana. “There is no safer space for Donald Trump to go in Arizona than Mohave County, which is full of disaffected former Californians and conspiracy theorists and ‘Don’t tread on me’ types,” said Barrett Marson, a Republican strategist in the state, referring to the county Trump is scheduled to visit Wednesday. Going to heavily Republican areas such as Bullhead City - or deeply red states such as Oklahoma, Alabama and Tennessee, as Trump has done in the last week and a half - is all but guaranteed to draw a friendly crowd, while still generating coverage in surrounding media markets and the national press, advisers say. Bullhead City is on the Arizona-Nevada border, and Trump’s appearance there could help mobilize Republican voters in Nevada, where GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo has only a narrow lead over his opponent. Rep. Elijah Crane (R) also faces a competitive race in Arizona’s neighboring 2nd Congressional District. Some choices are less strategic. New York conservative talk radio host Bob Lonsberry urged Trump to cancel Friday’s trip to Syracuse, fearing it would harm the candidate’s chances. “Stay away, Mr. President,” he wrote on social media. “The last thing Bruce Blakeman needs is a visit from you.” Other officials maintained that all provide some advantage, even if it is for a House race elsewhere in the state from where Trump is visiting, or a statewide race just over the border. The president combines political strategy with his personal preferences, such as accepting requests to campaign for friends such as Blakeman and Mike Mazzei, the GOP gubernatorial nominee in Oklahoma. Since Labor Day, Trump has made 14 stops in other states, not including visits to his golf clubs in New Jersey and Virginia. Of those, two were presidential battlegrounds in the last decade. In addition to political considerations, the president’s team faces logistical challenges in finding large and secure venues in rural places. He does not like to stay overnight except at his own properties, such as his hotel in Las Vegas. Three people with knowledge of the schedule said Trump’s stop in Tennessee was something of a placeholder - a rally planned around the main attraction for him that day, the Alabama-Georgia football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, which he ultimately did not attend because of Hurricane Isaias. The White House chose the location after Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s team had for months recommended it, given its proximity to Fort Campbell, home of the 101st Airborne Division, and the area’s population growth. Blackburn, now the GOP nominee for Tennessee governor, is working to maximize GOP turnout as an independent candidate threatens to lower her margins, but the longtime elected official is not seen as being at risk of losing her race. GOP strategists hope Trump’s stop there also boosts Republican congressional candidates running in seats redrawn this year by the state legislature. Two people involved in planning his schedule said there are no trips scheduled to Maine or New Hampshire. Trump is still scheduled to visit Michigan, a state whose Senate race he’s been vocal about, but early voting and other data could change that plan, one of his advisers said. Wherever the itinerary takes him, some of Trump’s most devoted fans are willing to follow. Blake Marnell, the longtime Trump rally-goer known online as “Brick Suit,” has been driving through the night, sometimes for 14 hours, to make it to almost all the rallies this month. In Durant, Oklahoma, supporters stood outside for hours in ponchos as a storm moved through the region on the day of Trump’s rally - which started two hours late due to weather delays. In San Antonio, supporters lined up before dawn for his evening rally on Wednesday. One man told a KENS5 reporter he had driven nine hours to be there. “I just love Trump. That’s why I came this week,” the man told the television reporter. “I didn’t have nothing better to do anyway.” Beside him, another man who arrived before sunrise observed that he was used to seeing longer lines. “I’m surprised we’re still pretty empty right now,” he said. Authorities say the suspected shooter took his own life before police arrived. The victims included the suspect's wife, children and grandchildren, according to officials. Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook on Oct. 12 identified the adult victims as Twila Tanner, 51; Angelina Stone, 24, who was eight months pregnant; Jonathan Stone, 19; Matthew Stone Jr., 21; Michelle Stone, 44; and Lora Roberts, 37, reported the Erie Times-News, part of the USA TODAY Network . Erie police also did not release the names of the children. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the suspect shot and killed six people inside the house on the evening of Oct. 9. The gunman then allegedly met two other women, including a family friend, outside the home after they arrived in a "state of distress," Lorah said, citing surveillance video. The gunman allegedly shot the two women before he reentered the home and shot himself, according to the police chief. Authorities have not determined a motive for the incident, which police are treating as a domestic situation because many of the victims are related and lived in the same home. No autopsies were performed on any of the victims or the suspect. Lorah said officers recovered a handgun that was legally registered to the suspect. item.title: Judge calls DOJ's defense of abrupt tree removal at D.C. golf course 'inexcusable'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jan Wolfe WASHINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - A US judge said on Monday that she was "furious" with Justice Department lawyers for their conduct in a lawsuit seeking to halt the Trump administration's takeover of a historic golf ‌course in Washington, saying it was "inexcusable" that hundreds of trees were removed from the course over the weekend. "More ‌than being upset and furious right now, I am just deeply disappointed in the government," US District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington told government lawyers during ​a court hearing. "On what universe did anyone in your office think this was acceptable?" Reyes said the abrupt removal of about 500 trees at East Potomac Golf Links, which began on Friday afternoon, was unacceptable because in May she had demanded that the government provide advance notice of any substantive construction work at the golf course. The Justice Department's failure to notify the preservationist group that filed the ‌lawsuit of the tree removal work "has cost the ⁠government all of its credibility" in the case, the judge said. Justice Department lawyer Marissa Piropato said during the hearing that government attorneys had done their best to gather details on tree removal so ⁠they could share them in a court filing. "You did not do your best," Reyes replied. "You did your absolute worst." Since taking office in January 2025, US President Donald Trump has targeted US cultural and historical institutions - from museums and monuments to national parks and arts centers - in ​an ​attempt to reshape them. The president announced plans last year to overhaul East ​Potomac Golf Links, a century-old public golf course ‌owned by the federal government and managed by the National Park Service, part of the Interior Department. Trump, a frequent golfer who owns several courses, has said he hopes the renovation will allow the course to host major tournaments. The DC Preservation League said in a February 2026 lawsuit that Trump was flouting environmental laws to "irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history" so he could "convert a public recreation space into an exclusive, high-end golf course." Reyes told Trump administration lawyers at a May hearing that there would ‌be "serious consequences" if major construction work began without prior court notification. In an ​October 9 court filing, the Trump administration asked Reyes to dismiss the litigation, ​saying it was premature because the "proposed project remains at ​an early and conceptual stage." Lawyers for the DC Preservation League asked Reyes on Sunday to issue ‌an emergency order blocking further tree removal at the ​course and requiring notice of any ​other irreparable modifications, saying that despite her May remarks more than 500 trees were removed on Saturday. Reyes issued a temporary order on Sunday that paused any tree removal until Tuesday morning, and indicated during Monday's hearing that she ​intended to extend the block for longer. Kevin Griess, ‌a National Park Service official, said at Monday's hearing that tree removal was intended to improve safety at ​the park and restore its original design, and was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump's ​ambitions for the course. (Reporting by Jan Wolfe; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/judge-blasts-trumps-doj-over-160408594.html
