item.title: At least 20 killed in week of attacks on Saudi airports, officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Saudi Arabia said Sunday that it would "respond decisively" against the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen a day after a strike on Riyadh's international airport brought the expanding Middle East conflict home to the Saudi capital. The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the attack and warned airlines against flying to Saudi airports, calling them "potential targets." Saturday's attack killed at least 12, according to Saudi officials, and the Indian Embassy in Riyadh said another person had died the following day from injuries sustained in that attack. More than 300 were wounded. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The attack revealed the vulnerability of the U.S. ally and the ramifications of the Trump administration's reluctance to openly help fight the Houthis more than seven months into Washington's war with Iran. Riyadh's airport is Saudi Arabia's second-largest for civilians and is frequently used by royals and visiting dignitaries, including President Donald Trump in his last visit to the kingdom. The airport was attacked again Sunday, igniting a fire and killing one person and injuring 11, Saudi aviation authorities said. Officials also confirmed a separate attack on another major airport on the country's east coast. The United States is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence support, analysts and U.S. officials say. But the administration has stopped short of the direct military assistance that officials in the kingdom and its allies in Yemen's internationally recognized government have sought. After Saturday's attack, Trump told reporters he was weighing whether to join Saudi strikes on the rebel group, later adding that the U.S. "has communication with the Houthis." A statement by the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Turki al-Maliki, called the attack on the passenger terminal a "full-fledged war crime." Among those killed or injured Saturday were passengers and airport employees, Maliki added. There was no immediate information on the one American killed in the attack. Footage broadcast on Saudi state media after the Saturday attack showed some of the injured in the hospital with severe burns and bandaged arms. "This was a brutal bombing that killed innocent people," Hasan Barqawi, whose son was among the 12 killed, told a state-owned TV station. The escalation comes at an increasingly turbulent time for the Middle East's aviation sector. Iran's attacks on Persian Gulf airports have kept some travelers away, and a FlyDubai co-pilot attempted to take over a Tel Aviv-bound plane in what the United Arab Emirates has said was an attempt to crash the aircraft into Ben-Gurion International Airport. In the wake of the Saudi airport attacks, foreign missions in the kingdom have urged their citizens not to use the Riyadh airport, with the U.S. Embassy saying employees needed special permission to do so. It later expanded the warning to two international airports on Saudi Arabia's east and west coasts. The Saudi Civil Defense did not issue a take-cover alert on its social media pages for Riyadh, and the airport told passengers only of the need to confirm flights before heading there. With the U.S. push for a deal to end its war with Iran stalled, the escalating conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia is further rattling energy markets and threatening to draw in more of the region ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November. Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House in Britain focusing on Yemen and the Persian Gulf, predicted that Trump would get involved because the attacks are tied to the larger Iranian response to the war. "Even if he wants to avoid it for the sake of the midterms, there is something more important for him," Muslimi said. "He is presenting himself to MAGA and to everyone as the guy who is taming Iran." Lack of action would be "humiliating for Trump, not just the Saudis," Muslimi said. Yoel Guzansky, a researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said there is pressure on Trump to act because oil exports are at risk and the kingdom has agreed to buy billions of dollars' worth of American weaponry. The Saturday attack was part of a string of Houthi strikes on airports across the kingdom this past week. The group also launched an offensive last month to wrest territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast near the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait from the Saudi-backed government as Iran steps up attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, reducing the amount of oil getting out. Elsewhere in Riyadh, in an apparent effort to project an image of normalcy, the kingdom on Sunday kicked off a days-long energy conference that gathered industry executives from around the world. Photos on social media showed a packed conference chamber. For some, life will never be the same. "We want this to stop," said Barqawi, whose son was killed in the attack. "I do not wish this on anyone." Rachel Chason contributed to this report. item.title: Oil theft is on the rise in U.S. shale country as thieves cash in on soaring prices
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The spike in oil prices since the Iran war began this year has attracted more thieves, and they are increasingly professional criminals. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 60% so far this year, and fuel prices have risen even more as global refining capacity has fallen due to the Mideast and Russia-Ukraine wars. While oil theft has long been a part of the industry, the problem has become prevalent enough for the Dallas Fed to ask about in its quarterly surveys. The latest one showed that nearly half of firms that are primarily focused in the Permian Basin said their operations have been impacted by theft in oil fields. By contrast, 86% of firms operating mostly outside the Permian said they were not impacted. The Permian is the heart of the oil patch and the epicenter of the shale revolution that has transformed the U.S. into an energy superpower. It stretches across the vast expanses of West Texas and southeastern New Mexico—and is dotted with drilling rigs, pipelines, trucks and other infrastructure necessities. That’s made the Permian a target-rich environment. And now that U.S. oil prices have been hovering around $100 a barrel lately, criminals can’t resist the payoff. According to the Dallas Fed survey, 32% of executives who were impacted by oil theft said it had increased slightly over the last 12 months, while 47% said it remained the same, and 22% said it decreased slightly or significantly. Nearly half of the oil executives (47%) said the most common form of theft was targeted and organized, while 42% described it as opportunistic petty theft. Still, the losses were relatively minimal, with 84% saying the financial impact of the theft was low. A year ago, the Dallas Fed asked a slightly different set of questions about theft, including what exactly was stolen: 61% said crude oil; 58% said piping, valves and wiring; 39% said equipment; 27% said tools; and 12% said construction equipment and vehicles. Theft can also be committed by other firms. In August, executives from a wastewater disposal company were charged with felony oil theft, money laundering and organized crime. It was part of an investigation dubbed Operation Black Market Basin that resulted in the seizure of more than $12 million in petroleum products, vehicles, cash and other assets, according to the Texas Railroad Commission , which regulates the industry. The investigation involved petroleum allegedly acquired and sold across Texas, New Mexico and Oklahoma, the commission added. And in April, federal prosecutors announced charges in a large-scale oil theft conspiracy in the Permian Basin to transport stolen crude oil across the New Mexico-Texas border for resale. Howard County Sheriff Stan Parker told Texas Public Radio in May that his county, which is near the Midland-Odessa oil hub, sees “probably over 1,000, 1,500 barrels of oil reported stolen every month.” “Our problem is we don’t know who’s supposed to be there and who’s not,” he added. “If I pulled up on a tank battery right now, I don’t know if you can be there or you’re not. I don’t know if you’re drawing water off of it. I don’t know if you’re pulling oil. It’s got very complicated.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com This article originally appeared on Fortune at https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-theft-rise-heart-u-222558567.html
